summary: Resource servers sometimes need stronger or more recent authentication than the access token represents. This document defines a way for a resource server to tell a client its token is not enough and how to meet the requirement. It also describes how a client can ask the authorization server for a particular authentication strength or recency.

eli5.summary: A bank lets you check your balance with a card but asks for a fingerprint to move big money. This lets a service say "prove it's you again, more strongly" when needed.

questions: what is oauth step up authentication
what does acr_values mean in oauth
subtitle: How an API can tell a client 'that login is not strong or fresh enough', and how the client asks for a better one.

tldr.problem: A resource server may need a stronger or more recent user authentication than the one behind the access token a client presents, and OAuth had no standard way to say so.
tldr.mechanism: The resource server rejects the request with the error insufficient_user_authentication plus acr_values and/or max_age in the WWW-Authenticate challenge. The client repeats those values in a new authorization request and gets a token that records how the user authenticated.
tldr.outcome: Resource servers, clients and authorization servers can interoperate on step up authentication with little extra work, because the authorization request parameters already exist in OpenID Connect.

today: RFC 9470 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2023, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Step Up Authentication
sections.content:
Normally an authorization server picks how to authenticate a user from things known in advance: the scopes requested, the resource, the identity of the client. That falls short when the API itself decides, request by request, what it needs. The RFC gives the example of an eCommerce API that wants a stronger authentication when the item being purchased exceeds a threshold, or an API that decides from its own risk evaluation that a more recent user authentication is required.

RFC 9470 adds a new error code, insufficient_user_authentication, to the ones defined by RFC 6750. It also adds two parameters, acr_values and max_age, to the Bearer challenge. The client can then pass the same two values to the authorization server in an authorization request, using the parameters defined by OpenID Connect.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a website decides halfway through that it wants to be more sure who you are. This gives it a polite, standard way to ask.

sections.title: The Step Up Flow
sections.content:
The RFC lays out six steps. The client already holds an access token for the protected resource.

  • The client requests the resource with its access token.
  • The resource server decides the authentication behind the token is too weak or too old, denies the request and returns a challenge with acr_values and/or max_age.
  • The client sends the user agent to the authorization server with an authorization request carrying those values.
  • The user authenticates as required, and the authorization server returns a new access token that contains or references information about the authentication event.
  • The client repeats the original request with the new token.
  • The resource server finds the authentication acceptable and returns the resource.

The RFC calls the resource server's judgment of how a token was obtained an authentication level. 'Level' and 'step up' are metaphors: there is no absolute, interoperable hierarchy of authentication methods. The new token also need not replace the old one. A client may keep tokens with different authentication levels and pick the right one for each call, and it must not inspect the content of an access token to learn about its authentication, because OAuth 2.0 treats access tokens as opaque to clients.
sections.eli5: You show your card, the shop says 'I need your fingerprint too', you go to the fingerprint desk, get a new stamp, and come back. The shop checks the stamp and lets you in.

sections.title: The Authentication Requirements Challenge
sections.content:
The new error value insufficient_user_authentication goes in the error parameter of the Bearer challenge, and of other OAuth schemes that use the same parameter, such as the ones in RFC 9449. It means the authentication event behind the presented token does not meet the resource's requirements. How the resource server decides this is out of scope.

Two WWW-Authenticate parameters carry the requirements:

  • acr_values: a space-separated string of authentication context class reference values, in order of preference. The resource requires one of them.
  • max_age: the allowable elapsed time in seconds since the last active authentication event, meaning a user interacting with the authorization server in response to a prompt. It must be a non-negative integer.

Both may appear in the same challenge. If the request also lacks required scopes, the server MAY include a scope attribute as described in RFC 6750.
sections.eli5: The shop's note says exactly what it wants: 'a stronger kind of check' (acr_values) or 'a check done in the last few seconds' (max_age).

sections.title: Authorization Request and Response
sections.content:
A client that receives the challenge SHOULD parse acr_values and max_age and use them in a new authorization request. Both are OPTIONAL parameters already defined in OpenID Connect Core, so this document changes nothing about how an authorization server processes them. Any authorization server implementing OpenID Connect can take part with little or no change.

On the response side the RFC builds on OpenID Connect. If the request carries max_age, the server MUST include auth_time. For acr_values, OpenID Connect lets the server choose how to treat the value, but for access tokens this RFC says the server SHOULD treat the requested acr as necessary. The value is put in the access token only if the authentication actually met it. Otherwise the request fails with the unmet_authentication_requirements error. The reason given is to stop clients from looping, with the server repeatedly issuing tokens the resource server already refused.
sections.eli5: Your app takes the shop's note to the identity desk. If the desk cannot do what the note asks, it says so right away, instead of handing you the same useless stamp again.

sections.title: Conveying Authentication Information in Tokens
sections.content:
To judge a token, the resource server must learn how the user authenticated. The RFC covers two common validation methods. With JWT access tokens (RFC 9068), the auth_time and acr claims carry the time and context of the user authentication. They are set at authentication time and do not change when the access token is renewed.

With token introspection (RFC 7662), the response gains two top-level members: acr, the authentication context class reference that was satisfied, and auth_time, a JSON number of seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z. Other token formats and validation methods are allowed by agreement but are out of scope.

An authorization server can advertise support by listing acr_values_supported in its metadata document (RFC 8414). Its presence signals that the server understands and honors acr_values and max_age.
sections.eli5: The new stamp has to say how and when you were checked, so the shop can read it and decide.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content: The RFC is frank that the user experience depends on the policies each resource server and authorization server pair sets, and those policies are out of scope. It is possible to impose requirements that users cannot meet or that give a poor experience. Prompts may require using several devices or devices with specific security properties. How a user satisfies a requirement, as opposed to which requirement applies, is not specified here.
sections.eli5: The rules for what the shop asks for are up to the shop. This only gives them a way to say it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of OAuth 2.0, JWT access tokens, Bearer WWW-Authenticate, token introspection and authorization server metadata all still apply. The RFC says it MUST NOT be used to position OAuth as an authentication protocol: it only reports how authentication happened, and relies on a separate authentication layer such as OpenID Connect for the mechanics.

The challenge itself can leak information. If a resource server asks for a high assurance level for some users but not others, that could point attackers to likely high-privilege users, for example for spearhead phishing. Implementers should take care over what they disclose. A resource server MAY return a challenge without checking that the token is valid, but that leaks the required properties to someone who has not proven they can obtain a token. Finally, because this lets a resource server trigger user interaction, authorization servers and clients should consider that a malicious resource server might abuse it.
sections.eli5: The shop's note might accidentally tell a stranger which customers get extra checks, so the shop should be careful what it writes on it.
